The lure of the loo: how restaurant bathroom design went wild
Plush or pared back, flatteringly lit or full-on disco camp, a TikTokkable loo is now part of the hospitality experience
Anthony Bourdain was typically forthright when it came to his expectations for the toilet facilities in a food business. “I won’t eat in a restaurant with filthy bathrooms,” wrote the late chef and author, in his seminal, turn-of-the-millennium memoir Kitchen Confidential. “This isn’t a hard call. They let you see the bathrooms. If the restaurant can’t be bothered to replace the puck in the urinal or keep the toilets and floors clean, then just imagine what their refrigeration and work spaces look like.” Setting aside the fact that, in later life, Bourdain softened his stance (“Some of the best food experiences I’ve ever had [have been in] places where they really don’t give a shit [about bathroom cleanliness],” were his words in a 2018 interview) his initial take tells us plenty about what the average customer historically demanded of restaurant restrooms. They needed to be clean. They needed to be functional. They needed, at a push, half-decent hand soap and the faint, reassuring waft of pine-scented floor cleaner.
Today, things could hardly be more different. Where once restaurant toilets tended to be a boring, unglamorous afterthought, in recent years, they have emerged as arguably the most unexpectedly attention-grabbing room in the building: atmospherically distinct sites of creativity and muscle-flexing design, where lavish amenities, bespoke lighting, custom soundscapes, selfie mirrors and all manner of other eye-catching flourishes abound, and are documented by social media channels, such as @LoosOfLondon (TikTok followers: 78k).
Nip off to spend a penny at Michelin-starred Timberyard in Edinburgh and you’ll be plunged into an atmospherically shadowy space, soundtracked by the discordant pops and burbles of grapes fermenting. Do the same at Oxford’s south-Indian spot Dosa Darlings or Soho’s neo-trattoria Osteria Vibrato and you’ll hear, respectively, Stephen Fry’s booming narration of the Harry Potter audiobooks and the swelling sound of opera. The practice of rigging lavatories with a disco soundtrack and flashing lights activated by a button – as seen at Barbara’s Bier Haus in Birmingham, plus outposts of Bavarian cabaret bar Albert’s Schloss – is so commonplace that it has almost become a cliche. From palatial TikTok-bait boudoirs (see the sprawling, uplit powder rooms in Mayfair’s Bacchanalia) and horror-themed mini cinemas (MeatLiquor spin-off BloodSports in London’s Covent Garden) to the unexplained shrine to former basketball player Dennis Rodman (there is genuinely one of these in London haute rotisserie joint Story Cellar), the world of modern restaurant bathrooms is in the grip of an unlikely, ever-intensifying arms race waged with luxury mouthwash dispensers, avant garde music, and soft-lit mirrors that are so flattering they might as well be enchanted. So how did we get here? And how far is too far, when it comes to turning these functional ablution chambers into noisy Instagram backdrops or giant art installations?
Naturally, social media has had a huge impact, pioneering toilet interiors – particularly the futuristic egg-pods at Mayfair brasserie-cum-gallery Sketch – showing other operators how to turn a utilitarian amenity into a canny, digital age attraction. Yet, beyond all the hastily installed flower walls and neon signs, there is another significant factor. Namely, a post-Covid, industry-wide shift towards dining spaces that are more immersive, memorable and unapologetically atmosphere-forward.
“We’ve become fascinated with the tiny details that add up to make a difference in a restaurant,” says Jo Radford, head sommelier and co-founder at Timberyard, and creator of its viniculture-themed bathrooms. “The amount of time that a guest is in the building with food in front of them is quite a small portion of their overall time with us, so we were looking at all those other touch points and how we could elevate things.” The result was the unexpected onslaught of scent, purposefully impeded sight (“environmental health told us that the lights might be so low that it wasn’t safe,” adds Radford with a sheepish chuckle) and sound that acts as both talking point and nudging link to the earthy seriousness of Timberyard’s wine programme. But the use of a wash of loud, discordant noises also serves another function. “It definitely helps in terms of audio privacy, ” he notes, highlighting the fact that a lot of these loud, characterful soundtrack choices often act as a kind of sonic veil against some of the grimmer realities of shared lavatories.
More generally, the seclusion and privacy afforded by toilet facilities – plus the access flex of a selfie from within a hot new opening – is something that restaurant interior designers and operators are identifying, leaning into and playing with. “The bathroom is a little space where you can take time to look after yourself and maybe muck around and have an Instagram moment,” says hospitality designer Russell Sage, a more than 20-year veteran of the industry with clients including Gordon Ramsay and Angela Hartnett. “It’s increasingly become about giving people their own time, getting the lighting right, and making sure they feel a million quid by the time they step back into the restaurant.”
Nowhere is this more true than at Lilibet’s, a maximalist seafood restaurant in Mayfair that Sage worked on ahead of its opening late last year. Beyond the fact that its gilded, azure-hued restrooms are inspired by the young Queen Elizabeth II’s love of decorative china (a whole new kind of “royal flush”), they also feature mirrors that are lengthening and slimming. “There have definitely been enquiries from people about whether they can buy one from us,” says Sage. “We just thought, people want to look fabulous, so let’s make a mirror that guarantees you look even more fabulous.”
Expensively wrought trick mirrors, opulent miniature spas and panoramic “loos with a view” like the ones atop 20 Stories in Manchester, many of the restrooms in this new wave default to the luxurious, but it’s notable that even smaller, scrappier businesses are getting in on the act. Cal McRae, owner of Zillennial-coded Dalston bar Ellie’s, had already been experimenting with time-sensitive crimson lighting and video installation, when he noticed an issue with one of the bar’s signature, budget-friendly cocktails. “We had these beautiful martini glasses that cost £7, the martinis themselves were £8, and by the end of the weekend the majority of these expensive glasses would be smashed all over the toilet floor,” he explains. “I was adamant that [we not use cheaper glasses] and that it was worth the cost, but by the end it was like, this is so stupid.” The solution was to build a custom martini-holder rack into the area above the sink; a feature that not only helped preserve Ellie’s glassware but became a much-photographed encapsulation of its dishevelled cool, written up in international publications like the hugely influential New York culture Substack Feed Me. “I was absolutely buzzing off the back of that,” says McRae. “And it was nice to find this practical solution to a problem, that was interesting from a design point of view and became a bit of a talking point.”
That Ellie’s viral martini-holders were needed in the first place reminds us of one of the abiding realities of toilets in restaurants and bars: they are often magnets for illicit behaviour, drunken damage, petty theft and other miscellaneous forms of unobserved wildness. “We’ve had someone rip off all the framing around the sink. And in the first week I heard about two people having sex in there which, honestly, is a massive achievement for a bar owner,” says McRae, laughing. Perhaps unsurprisingly, this tendency towards chaos and the basic importance of lavatories have caused some problems for this new generation of immersive facilities. Late last year, the Manchester branch of bougie steakhouse chain The Cut and Craft implemented a five minute time-limit on their Instagrammable toilets; this spring, veteran restaurateur Jeremy King revealed he’d had to ban filming and hire extra security at his Bayswater grand cafe, The Park, because of the number of influencers arriving with suitcases, tripods and sound systems for prolonged video shoots in the handsome, honey-toned restrooms. Even something as pointedly mischievous as the screamingly camp disco loos in branches of Albert’s Schloss – with two adjacent toilets in the ladies with a big “push for disco” button beside them – has needed occasional policing. “Now and again, we’ll get four girls going in there with a bottle of prosecco and there’ll be a big queue after 20 minutes,” says James Plant, head of openings and innovations at Albert’s Schloss. “So we make sure we have toilet attendants, to give them a gentle knock and a nudge.”
Yes, these “influencer bans” often become a handy bit of additional publicity for the restaurant, but does the need for them also show us that the trend for ostentatious loos and logo-embossed selfie mirrors in restaurants and bars may already be circling the drain? McRae, founder of a bar so cool it was the venue for Charli xcx’s wedding party, certainly thinks so. “I hate the idea of putting a bar or restaurant name on a mirror,” he says. “I understand that a lot of people that come in might put [a photo] on Instagram, and that can help build a following. But it just feels so forced.”
Conversely, Sage believes that the kind of amplified, TikTok-ready bathroom aesthetic he employed in Lilibet’s will only become more commonplace. “It’s the world that we’re in now,” he says. “Going to a restaurant is not a cheap business, so we owe it to people to give them a good experience, turn up the volume and really put on a show. Ten or 15 years ago it was all about exposed brick and how dreary we could make everything look. I loved it at the time, but we’re now in an era where people are in search of a little bit of glamour, fun and enjoyment.”
The truth probably lies somewhere in the middle. Even if there is an active retreat from disco lights, selfie mirrors and some of the more gimmicky plays for virality that have dominated the world of restaurant bathrooms in recent years, we’ve passed a point of no return when it comes to bathroom design. Plush or pointedly stripped back; flatteringly illuminated or cast in a sexy, candlelit gloom; fitted with a Bond villain-worthy tank of live piranhas (as at Nikkei-themed Mayfair spot Pirana), or ornamented with nothing more than stacked pyramids of loo paper. Even a quieter aesthetic choice is still an aesthetic choice. And in an economically pressured era when hospitality businesses have to use every marketing tool at their disposal, a bathroom that has to be experienced to be believed is both added value and a kind of irresistible, dangled lure.
“We want to give people a stolen moment,” says Radford. “There’s nothing like seeing one of our guests returning from the bathroom, turning to the rest of the table and saying: ‘You need to go downstairs and experience that.’” Expect to see more and more restaurateurs continuing to turn their own facilities into the kind of miniature worlds that spark this level of unexpected ardour and intrigue. And if your dining companion suddenly disappears mid-meal for a prolonged toilet break – well, it’s no longer guaranteed that it’s a bad sign.

Scorched leaves, wilted blooms, brittle stems... After a brutal heatwave, your garden may look more like a patch of botanical heartbreak than the lush oasis you remember. But don’t despair! Gardeners everywhere know a straightforward trick to help revive your plants after extreme heat—and with a little patience and some TLC, many of your green companions can bounce back, even if they currently look worse for wear.
Assess Before You Act
Plants can show all sorts of stress after several blazing hot spells—burned foliage, shriveled flowers, desiccated branches, or just overall weakness. Before grabbing those pruning shears or, more drastically, replanting, take a moment to truly look over your garden. Some plants may look utterly defeated, but you’d be surprised how resilient they can be once kinder weather returns.
Once the worst of the heat is over, plants may seem parched, with scorched leaves or dry stems. Don’t rush in immediately: let your garden soak up those gentle late-summer or early autumn showers if they come, and enjoy the milder temperatures before starting any rescue missions. So what should you actually do to help your garden bounce back?
The Step-by-Step Revival
Trim the dead: Start by cutting off all the dead bits—stems, leaves, whatever is clearly scorched—on perennials, annuals, and even your favorite aromatic plants. The same goes for shrubs. But resist the urge to pull anything out, even if it looks beyond hope: many plants are simply taking a survival nap during the heat.
Patience pays: Nature is full of defense mechanisms. Your first job is simply cleaning off all the fried or dry parts caused by blazing sun and lack of water. And then… wait. (Yes, the hardest part of gardening!)
If rain doesn’t materialise, offer your garden a few gentle watering sessions. Start slow with smaller amounts, allowing roots and soil to absorb the moisture without being overwhelmed. After a scorching summer, soil and roots need moisture deep down to recover.
Water at dawn or dusk, when evaporation is lowest, so roots and soil reap the rewards and you’re not just feeding the atmosphere.
Avoid wetting the foliage—focus on the base for maximum benefit.
Rejunenate Soil and Roots
After an entire summer of blazing sun, the soil is left compacted, depleted, and bone dry. Sometimes a crust even forms at the surface. Loosen it up gently with a rake or fork—this helps water reach deeper. On the surface, work in some well-rotted compost to lighten the texture and add nutrients.
Don’t forget to add an organic mulch—compost, leaf mould, or straw—around all your plants. This helps lock in the moisture from your watering or any rogue rainstorms and forms a barrier against further sun, especially during an “Indian summer” if the heat sticks around.
Replacing and Refreshing Weak Spots
Give it a few weeks. Some plants may still refuse to recover despite your best efforts, and that’s your sign to remove them. Better to fill those bare spots than leave soil exposed to sun, wind, or heavy rain.
As you replant, lightly loosen the soil and add a little more mature compost. Not yet ready for new plants? Cover the empty patches temporarily with mulch such as dead leaves, shredded bark, or straw—this protects the soil from drying out and preserves its life until you can plant something new.
Lawn & Containers: Handle with Care
A lawn that’s looking more yellow-brown and patchy than green isn’t necessarily down for the count. Don’t rush for grass seed! Often, fall showers will bring it back to life naturally. Use this period to scarify (rake) the lawn to remove moss or dried blades—this aerates it and encourages new growth. If you must mow, keep the blades high so you don’t expose the grass to more sun. And if the heatwave drags on, a light sprinkle of water will support recovery.
Container plants suffer even more than their in-ground cousins during a heatwave. Their soil dries faster, and roots feel the brunt of the heat. Tidy up dead foliage and gently rehydrate the soil—don’t leave them sitting in drowned saucers, though! Surface mulch helps keep their substrate fresh. Skip the fertilizer and don’t pull anything out, even if things look bleak. Above all, observe before acting. If the sun just won’t quit, move pots to partial shade to spare them another cycle of stress.
So remember: after a heatwave, patience, observation, and gradual care are your best allies. Your garden may look a bit battered now, but with the right steps, you’ll soon see signs of life returning. If only all problems could be solved with a little water and a mulch blanket!

Insight
How extreme heat impacts fuel handling, storage and delivery
One Friday evening in mid-August, after yet another long, hot week, a government-issued alert on our phones gave a clear but alarming message to not undertake “any activity that could start a fire”.
July was the hottest on record, with over two thirds of the UK in drought, and the risk of wildfires high. With exceptionally dry conditions, those working with flammable liquids such as fuel, need to be more vigilant than ever. Stewart Ower, Risk Management & Spill Response Lead for Compass Environmental spoke with Fuel Oil News to share important insight into managing associated risks.
At the depot
With large volumes of flammable liquids stored on site, one event could bring disaster for human health, the environment, your assets and your reputation. Whilst some risks may be obvious and easily managed, such as prohibiting smoking and bonfires on site, others are less apparent:
- Where you park matters: Parking your fleet close together may be space efficient but it brings higher risks of low-speed collisions or manoeuvring incidents. Should one vehicle catch fire or be set alight, the others may fall in a domino effect, wiping out your entire fleet and putting your business off the road. Space the tankers, spread the risk.
- Keep your boundaries clear: Consider the positioning of trees and vegetation in relation to your tank farm – what would happen if a wildfire approached your site? Creating a fire break around your depot can limit the damage from neighbouring wildfire risks.
- An empty tanker can be a safer tanker: Fully loaded tankers parked at the depot overnight could mean disaster if an incident happens out of hours. Keep heating oil and DERV tankers empty when not in use to minimise the risk should an incident occur.
- Limit high risk activities on site: Always conduct a thorough risk assessment and limit work which could cause sparks, for instance hot works – have a hot works permit system in place.
- Assess your office set up: The office is not without risks and should a fire start, the damage could spread to your fuel storage. Ensure your electrical systems are compliant, inspections are up to date and fire extinguishers are regularly serviced.
- Prepare your personnel: Regular fire drills and training are essential and can save lives – don’t skip them. Take this one step further and ensure the fire services are also familiar with your site layout and water supply points.
Some depot incidents are more unpredictable such as lightning strikes or even arson attacks. Having a fire risk management plan and DSEAR Assessment is a must, as is an environmental risk management plan with clear incident response strategies.
On the road
Leaving the depot comes with its own risks. During breaks, ask drivers to choose their spot wisely: with a tanker full of highly flammable liquid, be mindful of parking up next to woodlands, heathland or grasslands which may be extremely dry and vulnerable to wildfires.
Accidents can happen whatever the weather. With the recent New Forest wildfire starting from a van fire, even a breakdown could cause disaster in dry conditions. Should your drivers experience difficulties in transit, from major rollovers to minor breakdowns, ensure they act vigilantly and can identify risks to human health and the environment, avoid smoking near the vehicle and raise the alarm in the most appropriate manner.
Delivering to customers
Once your drivers have safely reached their destination, ensuring your team are trained and well versed in handling potential hazards is critical. Despite government limitations on risky activities such as bonfires and disposable barbecues, there is still a possibility these could have taken place. Watch out for hot embers when considering where to park or the path of the hose and be sure to prohibit smoking near the tanker, hose or oil tank.
When making deliveries, ensure tanks are filled no more than 90% as oil can expand in the heat causing overflow. Plastic oil tanks can be more likely to fail on the first fill following periods of hot weather due to the stress of high heat and sun exposure. With customers looking to fill their tanks over the coming months, brief your drivers to look for signs of damage and if in doubt, don’t deliver.
What if the worst happens?
When a serious fire occurs, having the right support in place can make a significant difference to how effectively the incident and its aftermath are managed.
For fuel distributors in particular, a major fire can quickly develop into a complex event involving emergency services, regulators, neighbouring properties, business interruption and potentially significant financial and reputational consequences.
A sector-specific insurance policy, such as Compass Environmental’s Oilshield Insurance and Risk Management scheme, can help manage the aftermath of a serious incident. With 24/7 incident support, this includes the coordination of elements such as arranging specialist contractors, liaising with regulators and other third parties, coordinating investigations and remedial works, and helping to move the incident through from the initial emergency response towards recovery and resolution.
However, effective risk management starts long before an incident occurs. Good site housekeeping, appropriate fuel storage, effective separation of ignition sources, suitable fire precautions, clear emergency procedures and regular staff training can all help to reduce both the likelihood and potential severity of a fire.
No business can remove risk entirely, but understanding where the vulnerabilities lie, putting sensible controls in place and having a clear plan for what happens if those controls fail can make a considerable difference when the worst happens.

On a hot day, you can tell your body is doing its job when you start to feel the sweat. When the body warms up — by even as little as half a degree — the brain tells the body to redirect blood flow toward the skin and the skin produces sweat. When the sweat evaporates, the body can release that heat, and your skin and body cool down.
But, these responses require the heart to pump harder and faster, and our bodies need more oxygen and water to keep up the cooling processes. These changes can cause heat stress, putting a strain on the heart, which can be dangerous, especially for the elderly and people with heart conditions and other illnesses.
Climate change is making things worse in a couple of different ways. First, climate change is causing heatwaves more frequently in Canada and other parts of the world. The heatwaves also lasting longer with both daytime and nighttime temperatures staying high for multiple days to weeks. This means people are at risk of heat stress more often and for longer.
Climate change is also causing these regions to experience higher temperatures than most people and communities are prepared for, especially in cities, which can be hotter than rural areas. Think of schools, community centres and hospitals that have not needed air conditioning in the past, but now need it.
It helps to know how to handle the heat. Know the early warning signs of heat stress, which can include excessive sweating and thirst, headache, dizziness, nausea, weakness and muscle cramps. Drink plenty of water, especially when exercising or doing outdoor activities. Find ways to cool down, such as moving into shade or cool spaces.
Also, keep an eye on your neighbours and check on people at greater risk, particularly older adults, young children and people with illnesses. Don’t be afraid to seek medical attention when it's needed, like when you notice confusion, fainting or seizures, which can mean heat stroke.
Glossary:
Sweat: the salty, clear liquid released through the skin's pores by special glands to help cool down the body
Heat exhaustion: illness that happens when your body overheats after experiencing high temperatures and heavy sweating
Heat stress: a condition that can occur when the body becomes hotter than its ability to reduce the heat (e.g., by sweating)
Heat stroke: a life-threatening medical emergency where the body overheats and fails to cool itself down

Airport union demands safety and transparency after worker dies in extreme heat
Summers are getting hotter in the Charlotte region, and outdoor workers are among the most vulnerable to heat illnesses. The 32BJ SEIU airport workers union held a vigil Thursday morning for a woman who advocates and coworkers say recently succumbed to the heat during her shift.
ABM worker Colleen Coates collapsed on a jet bridge at Charlotte Douglas International Airport on September 17, when high temperatures hit the 90s. She was waiting to clean an American Airlines plane, which contracts with ABM for cabin cleaning. Union organizer Seneca Davis said it was Coates' last plane before she could go home for the day.
“The jet bridge was really, really hot,” Davis said. “She couldn’t stand the heat, and she passed out.”
Medics could not resuscitate 55-year-old Coates. Her colleague, LaShonda Barber, said improving workplace safety at the airport is her top concern, but the company doesn’t take it seriously. She said the company is short-staffed and doesn’t provide adequate equipment for employees to perform their jobs safely.
“Our trash truck doesn’t even have air conditioning,” Barber said. “We’ve been suffering all summer long, moving so fast.”
Temperatures are rising, but worker protections are not
Barber described her friend as a hard worker and a “very caring person” who “talked to everybody.”
“She’s the one I would want on my team,” Barber said. “She wants the job done and done right.”
During the vigil, union representatives asked for greater transparency and more worker protections, including the right to call out when they’re sick.
Coates suffered from chronic health conditions and had been recently hospitalized. High temperatures can exacerbate existing health problems, such as respiratory and cardiovascular diseases. Davis said that Coates used an inhaler and took medications for high blood pressure.
ABM said in a statement that it supports airport workers affected by Coates’ passing but declined to comment on the circumstances.
“We are deeply saddened by the passing of our colleague, Colleen Coates, and extend our heartfelt condolences to her family, friends, and colleagues during this difficult time,” an ABM spokesperson said in a written statement to WFAE.
Barber said she was not aware of receiving any communication about her friend’s death from the company.
Zachary Turner is a climate reporter and author of the WFAE Climate News newsletter. He freelanced for radio and digital print, reporting on environmental issues in North Carolina.
